blocks.title: Messages on Invisible Waves
blocks.subtitle: Modulation, antennas, propagation and the limits set by noise

blocks.text:
Radio carries voices, pictures and data through empty space at the speed of light. A transmitter impresses information on an electromagnetic wave, an antenna launches it, and somewhere a receiver picks a few billionths of a watt out of the noise and recovers the message.

The principles have not changed since the first wireless telegraphs. What has changed is how close engineers now work to the theoretical limits.

blocks.heading: Carrier and modulation
blocks.text: A steady radio wave, the **carrier**, carries no information. Information is added by varying one of its properties in step with the message: its amplitude (AM), its frequency (FM) or its phase. Digital systems switch between a set of amplitude and phase states, each representing a group of bits.

steps.text: **Modulate.** The message, analogue or digital, alters the carrier's amplitude, frequency or phase.
**Radiate.** A power amplifier drives the antenna, which converts the electrical signal into a travelling electromagnetic wave.
**Propagate.** The wave spreads, weakens with distance, and is reflected, bent and absorbed by terrain, buildings and the atmosphere.
**Demodulate.** The receiver selects the wanted frequency, amplifies it and recovers the message from the carrier.

points.title: Source and coding
points.text: The message is digitised, compressed and protected with error-correcting codes.

points.title: Modulator
points.text: Maps the data onto the carrier wave.

points.title: Transmitter and antenna
points.text: Amplifies the signal and radiates it in the desired direction.

points.title: Channel
points.text: The path between the antennas, adding loss, fading, interference and noise.

points.title: Receiver
points.text: Filters, amplifies, demodulates and decodes to recover the data.

blocks.heading: The limit set by noise
blocks.text: Every receiver adds random noise, and no design can remove it entirely. Claude Shannon showed that a channel of a given bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio has a maximum rate at which data can be sent with arbitrarily few errors. Modern coding schemes come within a fraction of a decibel of that limit. To send more, a system needs more bandwidth, more signal power, or more antennas.

items.title: Frequency and wavelength
items.text: Related by the speed of light: higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

items.title: Modulation
items.text: Varying a carrier to carry information: AM, FM, PSK, QAM and others.

items.title: Bandwidth
items.text: The range of frequencies a signal occupies; wider bandwidth can carry more data.

items.title: Antenna gain
items.text: How strongly an antenna concentrates power in one direction.

items.title: Signal-to-noise ratio
items.text: Wanted signal power divided by noise power, usually given in decibels.

items.title: Multipath fading
items.text: Copies of a signal arriving by different paths and partly cancelling.

blocks.text: Radio engineering is the art of recovering a whisper sent from far away in a room full of noise.

blocks.heading: A finite resource
blocks.text: Radio spectrum cannot be manufactured. Every new service competes with existing ones for frequencies, and interference crosses borders, so allocation is coordinated internationally. Engineers respond with denser frequency reuse, directional and multiple antennas, higher frequencies and smarter sharing between users.

items.title: Telemetry
items.text: Data from balloons, rockets and remote instruments.

blocks.question: A radio wave has a frequency of 100 MHz. Its wavelength is about:
blocks.explanation: Wavelength is the speed of light divided by frequency: 300,000,000 m/s ÷ 100,000,000 Hz = 3 m.

blocks.question: According to Shannon, channel capacity increases with:
blocks.explanation: Capacity is bandwidth multiplied by the base-2 logarithm of one plus the signal-to-noise ratio.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Decibel (dB)**: a logarithmic ratio of powers. **Carrier**: the wave that is modulated. **Line of sight**: a direct path between antennas. **Ionosphere**: charged upper atmosphere that reflects some frequencies. **Bit error rate**: the fraction of bits received wrongly.
